From Goldie’s drum ’n’ bass record room to a surreal puppet shop, BEYOND THE STREETS brings six decades of street culture into one of London’s most prestigious art spaces.

From graffiti-covered subway carriages and underground photography to an immersive recreation of Goldie's legendary Metalheadz record shop, a major exhibition celebrating six decades of street culture has returned to London - and there's a lot to get stuck into.

There is a particular kind of energy that comes with street culture. It's rebellious, resourceful and often deliberately confrontational - born out of communities and creative movements that have historically existed outside the boundaries of traditional art institutions.

Now, the Saatchi Gallery is giving all of that a pretty sizeable showcase, with an exhibition spread across two floors and packed with hugely influential artists, photographers, musicians and activists who helped make these movements what they are today.

One of the first things to catch your eye as you step into the gallery is a recreation of a New York City subway carriage, covered in graffiti and paying homage to the movement that helped propel the art form into the international consciousness. Nearby, visitors can explore the history of graffiti through photographs, documents and fascinating ephemera, including crime reports and material documenting how public transport authorities attempted to tackle the proliferation of graffiti across their networks.

But the exhibition isn't just concerned with the origins of graffiti. It also explores the wider cultural ecosystem that grew around it, from the music and fashion to the photography and personalities that helped give the movement its identity.

For anyone interested in the history of British hip-hop, the photography of Normski is a particular standout section. Having documented the scene since the 1980s, his photographs capture a formative period in British music and youth culture, featuring everyone from Public Enemy and Rakim to homegrown artists such as MC Duke.

Among his personal highlights is a miniature exhibition he has constructed on a skateboard deck, featuring tiny reproductions of his own photographs arranged almost like a map through his own archive.

Speaking to Euronews Culture, he explained how he found his way into the scene: "Eventually, I got into editorial work, and hip-hop kind of found me. I found like-minded people in hip-hop and just went crazy taking pictures of all the gigs. Hip-hop has really been my real love because of the energy, the fact that it's real people, street people of all cultures, all coming together. Ultimately, it's about music. I love the music."

He was equally enthusiastic about the exhibition, describing it as "like a funfair" and adding: "I honestly think BEYOND THE STREETS is probably way past what you'd expect."

Another fascinating perspective comes from American photographer and filmmaker Estevan Oriol, whose work documents the streets of Los Angeles, particularly its Latino communities and gang culture.

Oriol, who began his career tour managing with legendary hip-hop groups including House of Pain and Cypress Hill, and spent decades photographing the city's streets and communities. His collection focuses particularly on Latino gang lettering, much of which dates back to the 1990s.

"What got me into it was just seeing the way they would write. It was so much different from regular graffiti or that type of street culture. With gang graffiti, it's not a colourful thing. They just want you to see it. They want it black, they want it bold, and that's kind of why they chose Old English."

Another of the exhibition's biggest draws is an entire room dedicated to British music icon Goldie. Before becoming one of the defining figures of jungle and drum and bass, Goldie made his name as a graffiti artist in the West Midlands.

Growing up in Wolverhampton, he discovered graffiti and breakdancing as a teenager, developing an artistic identity that would eventually take him from Birmingham's streets to the international music scene.

The centrepiece is an immersive recreation of a Metalheadz record shop, paying tribute to the influential drum and bass label Goldie founded in 1994. Visitors can wander through the installation, which is filled with records and music memorabilia, while 30 stacks of vintage TVs show three decades of short films and music videos from his career.

There's also a wonderfully unexpected contribution from British artist Lucy Sparrow, who has recreated a graffiti artist's studio entirely in felt. Set inside a disused Tube station, it's filled with handmade spray cans, graffiti-covered walls, tags and all the usual tools of the trade, only everything has been given Sparrow's trademark soft, stitched treatment.

Sparrow told Euronews Culture that she had spent three months working on the project, followed by four days installing it at the gallery.

A long-time admirer of the graffiti scene, she said she wanted to bring London-based writers like 10FOOT and TOX26 together with international artists, explaining that it was "great turning and interpreting that world into my world of felt."

Elsewhere, you'll find work from some pretty big names, including FUTURA 2000, Damien Hirst, Shepard Fairey, KAWS and Jenny Holzer, alongside the archive of The Big Issue and photographs documenting everything from British punk to the rise of hip-hop.

There's a real mix of things to look at, and that's part of the fun. Some rooms feel like traditional galleries, while others are more like stepping into a different world altogether. And while the exhibition occasionally feels overwhelming in the sheer volume of material on display, that's arguably part of its appeal.

The good news is that the BEYOND THE STREETS exhibition runs until 5 May 2027, so there's plenty of time to see it. And you might even want to go back for a second look.

Seeking out lesser-known neighbourhoods, booking beekeeping experiences, and learning a local game while on holiday are among the hidden trends set to shape travel in 2027.

With a new year just around the corner, what will shape the way we travel in 2027? There’s already been a host of predictions issued by travel companies and experts, and now some “hidden” trends have been unveiled.

According to a report from GetYourGuide, the “holidaymaxxing” trend of squeezing in as much as possible into one trip is “out” and is giving way to a slower, spontaneous approach, with travellers increasingly keen on "getting lost in the moment".

The online travel experiences platform surveyed 10,157 people across seven markets – the US, UK, France, Spain, Italy, Germany and Japan – for its annual Hidden Trends report. Drawing on millions of bookings alongside the survey findings, it revealed that 78% of travellers feel that “a truly restorative holiday means ditching the schedule”.

Almost one in three respondents said they leave their smartwatches at home, with tech being used for trip planning (56%) and then truly switching off while away.

The company calls it “antioptimisation: plan hard, then let go” while Anne Wallin, Global Trends and Experiences expert at GetYourGuide added that travellers aren’t “planning less”, they’re “planning differently”.

She added: “Eight in 10 want a holiday free from a schedule, so instead of cramming in a must-see list, they’re choosing a few experiences to go deep on. Our Hidden Trends points to a shift away from optimisation culture to a deeper and more meaningful travel experience.”

The hidden trends for 2027

The research identified five new traveller archetypes, which form the hidden trends that could redefine how we will travel come 2027.

‘The Scentualists’

We’ve all heard the phrase “take a picture or it didn’t happen”, but travellers may soon look to bottle up their holiday memories through scents rather than other souvenirs.

GetYourGuide found that 56% of respondents would be willing to pay for scent-based experiences, such as a perfume masterclass or a guided workshop. This trend is especially popular among Gen Z (69%) and Millennial travellers (65%).

Further, 77% of respondents also said that a single scent can transport them back to a past holiday, with booking data finding that scent-related experiences have surged 114% year-on-year.

‘The Fermentors’

Amid an era of chronically being online, slowing down and embracing patience is a new luxury, according to the report. From experiences such as crafting their own kombucha or attending a kimchi cookery class, 72% of respondents said they're "fascinated" by watching food made from scratch.

A further 71% said that understanding the origins of food added "deeper value" to their travel. Among Millennials, 58% have booked getaways specifically to experience local food production.

GetYourGuide’s booking data also found that balsamic and vinegar production workshops climbed by 73% year-on-year.

‘The Detourists’

The detouring trend is all about heading to world famous destinations, but swapping popular tourist spots and experiences for lesser-known alternatives.

Set to become popular in 2027, 61% of respondents said they're more likely to deliberately seek lesser-known local neighbourhoods compared to five years ago. This trend is even more popular among Gen Z (72%) and Millennial travellers (69%).

‘The Players’

For the generation raised on online gaming, the next travel activity might be something they can’t download, as 62% said they would consider learning a local game while on holiday.

This willingness is even more pronounced among tech-savvy Gen Z, with 78% open to the idea. This suggests a generation defined by digital play is "keen to connect with local cultures by seeking out the analogue version".

‘The Pollinators’

According to the research, travellers will swarm towards apiaries to learn about beekeeping while away, offering another opportunity to gain patience and slow down.

"Pollinator tourism" is becoming less of a niche curiosity and more of a mainstream travel trend, GetYourGuide said, with its internal data finding that bookings for these experiences have grown 65% year-on-year. Meanwhile, 50% of respondents also said they would consider beekeeping when on holiday.

In 2005, a programming error unleashed a plague in World of Warcraft that epidemiologists used to study people's behaviour during an outbreak, later revived by COVID-19.

Return to classic Azeroth. That was the promise with which Blizzard launched 'World of Warcraft Forever' to the world on 4 November. For some, it meant a return to an earlier time, using nostalgia as a sales engine, but for others that period is tied to a pandemic.

In September 2005 a programming bug turned the spell Corrupted Blood, designed for a single fight in the game against a dungeon boss, into a contagious disease that spread through the game's virtual cities. The glitch ended up killing thousands of characters and, two years later, made the cover of 'The Lancet Infectious Diseases'.

Epidemiologists experienced in Azeroth something that could not have been replicated in any other way. The health professionals' models can calculate perfectly how a pathogen passes from one person to another, but not human behaviour or what people do when they know they might be infected. And without anyone having planned it, millions of players were showing it live.

How Corrupted Blood spread

It all began on 13 September with patch 1.6 and the opening of the Zul'Gurub raid dungeon for 20 players. Its final boss, Hakkar, cast Corrupted Blood, an effect that drained health every few seconds and spread to anyone nearby. Inside the raid it was just another obstacle that could be managed but was not supposed to leave that space. Outside it simply was not meant to exist.

But it escaped through the pets of two classes. Both hunters and warlocks could dismiss their pets while they were infected and then summon them again in a capital city, where the effect reappeared unchanged. From a player's point of view it was an annoyance, but from an epidemiologist's it was a textbook zoonosis, a pathogen that jumps from animals to people and back again, with pets acting as a reservoir.

The non-player characters controlled by the game itself (the so-called NPCs), such as guards and vendors, became infected but did not fall ill, so they were immortal and asymptomatic. They were symptomless carriers placed in the busiest spots. The Typhoid Mary of Ironforge was a guard.

Transport was all that was missing, and the game made it easy. Every person could travel from one city to another instantly, and many did so while infected. Eric Lofgren and Nina Fefferman, authors of the 'The Lancet' study, compared that leap with plague travelling alongside Mongol armies or with 19th-century cholera. In the packed capital cities transmission depended on crowd density, as in any real city. They calculated that in those hubs the reproduction rate reached 100 infections per hour, a figure they themselves considered impossible for a real pathogen.

For a high-level character (with real pathogens this would be a middle-aged person without underlying conditions), the disease was little more than a cold. For a low-level one (people with illnesses, older people...) it meant dying in a couple of seconds. As in so many epidemics, the most vulnerable were hit hardest.

'World of Warcraft' had more than four million subscribers at the time. On 16 September Blizzard acknowledged on its forums that it was aware of the problem and tried what any health authority would have done, putting up quarantine barriers around the areas most affected.

It did not work. The disease was too contagious, it was impossible to truly seal off part of the map and the players were not willing to cooperate. In the end the company used a tool that no Ministry of Health has available and restarted the world. After several complete server resets and a patch that made pets immune, the outbreak was declared eradicated on 8 October.

What Corrupted Blood taught epidemiology

According to the most repeated version, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in the United States even asked Blizzard for data on the outbreak, convinced that it was a deliberate simulation. There was nothing they could be given. It had been an accident and nobody had recorded the spread.

The studies arrived in 2007. In March, Israeli epidemiologist Ran Balicer of Ben-Gurion University of the Negev pointed out in the journal 'Epidemiology (source in Spanish)' the parallels with bird flu, in which birds such as ducks carry the virus without becoming ill.

He also found similarities with SARS, which between 2002 and 2004 jumped from one country to another on board aircraft. In September, Lofgren, then a student at Tufts University who had lived through the outbreak with his own character, published with his supervisor Fefferman the cover article in 'The Lancet Infectious Diseases'.

These studies started from a known limitation. Computer models allow experiments with virtual populations, but they do not predict what each individual will do, and releasing a real pathogen just to observe it is unthinkable. In 'World of Warcraft', by contrast, players were very attached to characters into which they had put hundreds of hours. Their economic and social behaviour looked quite similar to the way they acted off-screen.

The proposal went beyond that particular case. They called for outbreaks deliberately designed with known parameters and built into the game without breaking it. The servers would record what proportion of infections came through each route, and the experiment would be repeated in different player populations to check the results. Consent could be obtained through licence agreements, although they admitted that privacy and anonymity would still be a problem. They also acknowledged the most obvious limit: in a game, death is fixed with a bit of patience.

Human behaviour in a pandemic, Azeroth-style

What was seen during those weeks now sounds very familiar. Many players fled the cities or stopped logging in. Healers went to the outbreak zones as first responders.

According to the authors, they probably reduced mortality, but they also prolonged the epidemic by keeping infected people alive. The possibility of resurrection encouraged people to take more risks, something that in public health is known as risk compensation (people tend to be more cautious when the risk is higher and less cautious when it is lower).

Some went to take a look and came away infected, a profile any journalist will find uncomfortably familiar. Others deliberately infected themselves and ran towards the busiest spots. This last group even attracted interest from US terrorism researchers, who saw in their behaviour a way to refine their models of how attackers make decisions.

Sceptics were not lacking. Several researchers doubted that what someone does with a dwarf on a screen is comparable to what they would do in the street, especially when dying only means running back as a ghost to your own corpse.

From Azeroth to Covid-19

In March 2020, with half the planet in lockdown, the study on Corrupted Blood returned to the spotlight. Lofgren, now at Washington State University, and Fefferman, at the University of Tennessee in Knoxville, found themselves explaining it again, this time with a real outbreak in the background. The parallels were apparent.

Asymptomatic carriers stopped being an Azeroth curiosity and became one of the major headaches of Covid-19. Health workers acted as overwhelmed first responders. To the old objection that in real life nobody infects others on purpose one could respond with presenteeism at work, the habit of going to work while ill so as not to let the team down, done without bad intentions but with similar effects.

The coincidence had a streak of dark humour. Zul'Gurub arrived in 'WoW Classic', the official rerelease of the original game, in April 2020, in the middle of lockdown. There was no plague, because Classic runs on code written after the pet bug had been fixed.

That same month Elysium, an unofficial server that keeps the original 'WoW' alive, did what Blizzard had never done. It quietly launched Pandemic in Azeroth, a deliberate epidemic that began with an infected item and a patient zero. The virus reduced characters' stats by 5% and their speed by 10%.

According to data published by its administrators, the infection reached 88% of players while there were no preventive measures. It fell to 42.2% when handwashing and distancing, among other measures, were introduced. It was not a scientific study, but it comes quite close to the controlled outbreak Lofgren and Fefferman had called for.

Outside Azeroth the idea has spread above all in classrooms. Whyville, a virtual world for children aged between 8 and 16, suffers an annual outbreak of Whypox, an imaginary smallpox that changes avatars' appearance and makes conversation harder. Researcher Yasmin Kafai studied for years how users reacted, and in 2021 her team designed Spikey-20, a virtual epidemic to teach young people how to seek information and protect themselves.

'Operation Outbreak' was created in 2015, in the middle of an Ebola epidemic in West Africa. It was driven by a Florida professor, Todd Brown, and Pardis Sabeti's lab at the Broad Institute at MIT and Harvard. An app transmits a fictitious pathogen via Bluetooth between nearby phones, and students then have to contain it. In 2020 it was presented as a tool to reopen schools more safely, and it also automatically records data that almost never get collected in real outbreaks.

The best-known case is 'Plague Inc.', a game in which the objective is to wipe out humanity with a pathogen. In 2013 the CDC invited its creator, James Vaughan, to give a talk. In January 2020 downloads surged in China, and by late February the authorities had removed it from the country's app store. In November that year his studio released 'Plague Inc: The Cure', a mode in which the goal is to stop the pandemic. It was developed with the WHO and was made free until Covid-19 was under control.

The plagues that came afterwards

Blizzard did not forget the episode. In October 2008, before launching 'Wrath of the Lich King', it programmed its own epidemic. Crates in Booty Bay infected players and turned them into zombies if nobody healed them in time. It cut the event short in less than a week, after complaints from those who just wanted to visit the bank.

Accidental leaks have not disappeared either. In July this year, Withering Contagion, a contagious effect from a Dragonflight dungeon, appeared in the middle of Stormwind on the US server Moon Guard, until Blizzard fixed it with a patch.

Now, since the launch of 'WoW Forever' two weeks ago, the veterans of 2005 have been eyeing hunters' pets warily, just in case.

Democrats will control 56 seats in the 100-seat Senate which will give them the power to block legislation, launch broad investigations into Trump's administration and thwart his judicial and senior government appointments.

Democrat Mary Peltola flipped the US Senate seat in Alaska on Tuesday after a tight race that unseated Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan, according to the official ballot count.

With 50.12% of the vote, Peltola's win means the US Senate will have a 56-44 Democratic majority, clinching the chamber's last open race in a midterm election that crushed Republicans across the country and handed US President Donald Trump a firm rebuke of his second term.

"As our next United States Senator, I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska's working families," Peltola said in a statement late on Tuesday.

"As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honour than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs and put Alaska first."

With far-flung rural voters in remote villages, the vote count in Alaska took two weeks to complete, but offered Peltola a strong mandate.

With 144,302 votes, Peltola beat Sullivan's 131,844 votes, even when combined with a second candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. who earned 4,760 votes.

Trump had called for another Republican candidate in the race, Gerald Heikes, to have his votes "immediately given" to Dan S. Sullivan, calling it the "fair solution."

Heikes won 6,105 votes in the race, but merging all the votes that Trump wanted to combine would still not have been enough to beat Peltola.

Dan Sullivan controversy

The Alaska Senate race had attracted national attention following a New York Times investigation revealing that aides to Peltola had recruited another man named Dan Sullivan to run for office with the goal of siphoning votes from the Republican incumbent.

"My opponent's campaign is literally focused on misleading Alaskans, lying and cheating," Senator Sullivan told reporters in Anchorage on election day.

Peltola has denied any knowledge of the alleged plot.

The fact that there were two candidates named Dan Sullivan had repeatedly drawn the ire of Trump, who said Democrats had used a "decoy" to siphon votes from the Republican candidate.

The Trump administration had gone so far as to ask the courts to block certification of the results if the incumbent Sullivan lost because of the potential mix-up.

The legal bid, which Trump has said he ordered personally, sparked alarm in political circles, but was dismissed by a federal judge ahead of the election.

However, US Attorney Michael Heyman claimed federal investigators were conducting both criminal and civil probes involving the Alaska Senate race.

Peltola's historic victory makes her one of the first two Native American women ever to be elected to the US Senate, where she will join Minnesota Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan.

Democrats will control 56 seats in the 100-seat Senate which will give them the power to block legislation, launch broad investigations into Trump's administration and thwart his judicial and senior government appointments.

The Claude maker is expected to set its IPO price on Wednesday before a Nasdaq debut on Thursday. Retail investors in France, Germany and other European markets can apply through participating brokers.

Anthropic is expected to price its blockbuster initial public offering on Wednesday, giving retail investors a chance to buy into the maker of Claude and testing Wall Street’s appetite for the companies behind the artificial intelligence boom.

AI stocks have swung sharply as investors question whether heavy spending on the technology will pay off. Wall Street is also weighing the prospect of tougher scrutiny of the industry after Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress in the midterm elections.

Nvidia, the chipmaker at the centre of the AI buildout and an early investor in Anthropic, has been shaken by the resignation of chief executive Jensen Huang after he admitted to an affair with a woman whom US intelligence reportedly believes could be a Chinese spy.

What European investors need to know

Anthropic’s latest US filing says the offering will comprise 825 million shares at an indicative price of $70 to $78 each.

Anthropic and its underwriters are expected to set the final offer price on Wednesday, US Eastern time. The company plans to publish it on its IPO website. The Wall Street Journal reported that strong demand could push it above $80 a share.

Retail investors in nine European Economic Area countries, including France, Germany and Spain, can apply through participating brokers. Anthropic’s European prospectus lists 4pm CET on Wednesday as the indicative deadline for retail orders.

Trading is expected to begin on Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT. Anthropic says brokers will confirm allocations that day. Investors who receive an allocation pay the IPO price. Those who buy once trading starts pay the prevailing market price. SpaceX shares rose 19% on their first day of trading in June.

Investors could also gain exposure to Anthropic through index funds. MSCI says it could add the Claude maker to its global equity indices as early as 1 December if it meets the eligibility criteria. Bloomberg reported that Anthropic could join the Nasdaq-100 on 21 December. Inclusion would prompt funds that track those indices to buy the shares, creating another source of demand in the weeks after the IPO.

How much could Anthropic raise?

At the top of the indicative range, the offering would raise about $64.4bn (€58.6bn), including shares sold by existing shareholders and before any additional shares are sold. That price would value the San Francisco-based company at about $1.4tn (€1.27tn), including employee stock options and restricted shares.

That would put it below the record $85.7bn (€78bn) SpaceX raised in June after its underwriters bought additional shares.

According to the filing, Anthropic’s revenue reached $17bn (€15.5bn) in the third quarter, up from $1.4bn (€1.3bn) a year earlier. Its annualised revenue run rate, a measure that projects recent sales over a full year, reached about $81bn (€73.7bn) on 31 October, up $10bn (€9.1bn) from the end of September.

Seven technology companies, including Google, Nvidia, AMD and Microsoft, have agreed to buy $26bn (€23.7bn) of non-voting shares at the IPO price in a separate private placement.

Siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, now Anthropic’s chief executive and president, founded the company with several colleagues in 2021 after leaving ChatGPT maker OpenAI.

The seven co-founders have pledged to donate 80% of their personal equity to philanthropic causes. Anthropic says about 20% of its shares will be dedicated to public purposes through those pledges, an employee donation-matching programme and a new public benefit fund.

According to an analysis by SaaStr, a software industry publication, Anthropic's more than 5,000 employees are set to bank more than $200 billion in the IPO, a windfall that could ripple through the San Francisco economy.

Anthropic flags AI and regulatory risks

Anthropic’s IPO filing warns that advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks if developed or used irresponsibly. It also says the company’s positions on AI regulation and safety could expose it to political backlash or disproportionate regulatory action.

The filing cites Anthropic’s dispute with the Trump administration. In February, Trump directed federal agencies to stop using Anthropic’s technology, and the Pentagon designated it a supply-chain risk after the company opposed the use of Claude for mass domestic surveillance or fully autonomous weapons.

Anthropic challenged the measures in court. A federal district court largely sided with the company, while a separate appeals court ruling upheld one of the Pentagon’s designations.

German aerial photographer Tom Hegen has documented the energy transition from Chile’s lithium-rich Atacama Desert to the nickel-processing complexes of Sulawesi, Indonesia.

Electrification has been hailed a “planetary ice pack” with the potential to ease global warming. How that electricity should be generated is a subject of fierce debate – but that’s not the only concern.

Behind every electric car, wind turbine and battery are critical minerals mined from the ground, often in vulnerable nations far from the people who use them.

German aerial photographer Tom Hegen has documented the energy transition from the skies since 2021, from Chile’s lithium-rich Atacama Desert to the nickel-processing complexes of Sulawesi, Indonesia.

His new book, ‘The Mineral Age’, aims to close the gap between the products we buy and the places they come from, and to draw attention to human rights abuses that underpin the energy transition.

“From the ground, you can’t really see much. They’re fenced off, and it’s such a huge area you don’t get the overview… When I’m up in the air, the entire landscape opens up,” Hegen tells Euronews Earth in an exclusive interview.

What are critical minerals used for – and where are they found?

Critical minerals are essential raw materials used in modern technologies and defence.

Electric vehicles (EVs) and energy storage batteries wouldn’t work without lithium, nickel, cobalt and graphite.

Bolivia, Argentina and Chile – known as the ‘Lithium Triangle’ – together hold more than half of the world's estimated lithium reserves. Indonesia is currently thought to hold the largest recoverable nickel reserves at 42 per cent, while the Democratic Republic of Congo is home to around half of all cobalt, with one in six children in DRC mining communities victims of child labour.

EV motors and wind turbine generators also rely on rare earths for their powerful magnets. Rare earths refers to a group of 17 chemically similar metallic elements that are abundant in Earth’s crust but rarely found in concentrated, mineable deposits. China has the world’s largest reserves of rare earth elements at 50 per cent and plays a major role in their processing, at 76 per cent.

Copper, valued for its electrical and thermal conductivity, is used to carry energy through wiring, circuit boards and chips.

As clean technologies gain pace – alongside missile construction, AI data centres and consumer electronics, which also rely on critical minerals – demand for these materials is soaring.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) expects it to almost double by 2040 under current policies, with demand for lithium more than tripling. The ‘35-by-35’ Global Electrification Pledge being debated at COP31 could push those numbers yet higher.

According to forecasts by Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, at least 384 new mines will be needed globally by 2035 to meet demand for electric vehicles and energy storage batteries alone.

One 2022 study found that more than half of energy transition mining projects were on or near Indigenous peoples’ lands. Often, the places richest in critical minerals are also those most vulnerable to climate impacts like extreme weather, compounding the risks for local communities.

‘The legacy is forever’: The human impact of critical mineral mining

For those living in the shadow of South America’s lithium fields, the DRC’s cobalt and copper mines, and Indonesia’s nickel and tin operations, the dark side of our electric future is all too clear.

On the sidelines of COP31, Indigenous leaders are sounding the alarm: “They want to accelerate new technology and mining, but not at the speed of rights,” Indigenous activist Edson Krenak tells Euronews Earth.

“One of the doctrines created to lead this energy transition is called ‘just transition’, but it is not ‘just’ on the ground,” says Krenak, who is an advocacy coordinator at Indigenous-led nonprofit Cultural Survival. “We are seeing the rights of communities sacrificed, violated, for the rights of the rich… to have their so-called clean energy.”

Krenak’s people, from Minas Gerais in Brazil, are still living with the fallout of the deadly 2015 Mariana and 2019 Brumadinho disasters. When these iron ore tailings dams collapsed, they killed hundreds of people, unleashed heavy metals-laden toxic sludge that continues to poison survivors, destroyed livelihoods and dismantled traditional ways of life.

Now lithium mines are moving in: Krenak says communities in the Jequitinhonha Valley have reported dust, water contamination and blasting near schools and villages for years, while investors and authorities rely on impact assessments submitted by the mining companies themselves.

“The legacy is forever, because it usually takes 200, 300 years to recover the environment,” says Krenak. He adds that communities are rarely made aware that tailings dams, which store the waste leftover after minerals are extracted, remain and must be managed indefinitely after mining operations end. Hegen documents these human-made landforms in his book, with examples from the US to Spain to Chile.

‘We are part of the problem with our consumption’

Thousands of kilometres away, Europeans are shielding themselves from the energy crisis with solar, wind power and EVs. While this has helped to curb planet-heating emissions, moving from a fuel-based to mineral-based energy system comes with its own fallouts.

Krenak says he “fully supports the energy transition” – “There’s no doubt we need transformation,” he says, “but we also need transformation on the demand side”.

“Everyone who uses a phone, a laptop, an EV, whatever it is, we are part of the problem in a way with our consumption, and we should be aware that people in other countries suffer from mining these metals,” says Hegen, who hopes to spark discussion and rethinking through his photography.

How can we handle critical minerals more responsibly?

Hegen believes the energy transition is “the only way forward” but he urges against “repeating the mistakes we made in the past, where we exploited other countries for resources and other people suffered from it”.

While we can all play our part in curbing demand for energy and products, greater oversight and accountability is needed on the ground.

Although international governance of transition mineral mining has made strides in recent years, including through the G7’s 2025 Critical Minerals Action Plan to advance standards-based markets and the EU’s Critical Raw Materials Act, it remains fragmented and non-binding.

Intense pushback from China and Russia saw language on transition minerals excluded from the final COP30 text last year, leaving scant hope for this year’s deal.

“We need reinforcement of the regulations and the laws that exist in Brazil and many other countries to keep our community safe,” says Krenak, emphasising the need for independent assessments separate from the mining companies’ own reports.

Financial institutions with mineral investments could also add pressure by setting requirements on deforestation, hazardous waste management, social protections and remedying harms.

“There is no doubt: we must decarbonise our economies and the way we live,” Hegen writes in his book. “This requires a shift away from consumable fossil fuels, extracted and burned once, toward a system based on durable metals that can, and should, be reused.”

As well as stronger regulation, better enforcement and more transparent supply chains, the solution lies in improving product longevity and circular design.

“A phone is really hard to recycle. Batteries are really hard to recycle,” Hegen tells Euronews Earth. “Products should be designed today, even more so, so they can be recycled, because all these metals have been mined already.”

Hope may also rest in future innovations such as synthetic lab-engineered alternatives for critical minerals and specialised plants that naturally extract metals from the soil.

More and more events occur that are not classic military actions yet still threaten our security, from state-sponsored cyberattacks to climate change and global pandemics.

Supermarket refrigerators heated to 50 degrees by hackers. Grain ships destroyed by drones in the Black Sea, and water shortages in the Carpathian Basin that endanger tourism, farming and electricity supplies. Incidents like these, caused by methods outside classical warfare, have become more frequent in recent months.

Researchers at the Global Security Research Group, part of the Institute of Global Studies at Corvinus University of Budapest, have recorded more than 50 so-called non-traditional security challenges in Central and Eastern Europe since October.

The database is open to the public on the Geo-Polemic Substack page, and its creators say they will update it regularly.

The group’s leader says the region is being hit at the same time by the effects of climate change and the war in Ukraine.

“I would not say that this region necessarily stands far out from the field in some way, but it is important from this point of view because of its specific vulnerabilities,” Péter Marton told Euronews.

Marton pointed to demographic challenges, ageing critical infrastructure and a level of energy dependence that is significant by comparison with other regions. “This justifies giving special attention to this region,” he said.

State actors behind more than half of incidents

An associate professor at Corvinus, Marton said state actors were responsible for more than half of the incidents the team collected.

“Using military means, even in a way that is completely denied, damage can be inflicted on others with non-conventional methods,” he said, citing the Black Sea, where ships have been damaged and sunk.

“It is particularly sad to see significant grain shipments being lost when the state of global food supply is anything but reassuring. Only yesterday a shipment of 3,000 metric tonnes of grain was lost with a ship in Bulgarian territorial waters.”

Russia’s hybrid war features heavily in the news, but it is not the only state active in Europe. France, for example, has accused Iran of carrying out the cyberattack on its supermarket refrigeration systems.

Climate, energy and crime also count

Non-state actors also play a major role, according to Marton. “After the summer of 2026 it is easy to recognise what kind of threat climate change can pose, or what kind of threat energy dependence and reliance on energy imports can mean for the economy,” he said.

Organised crime, terrorism and many other factors also fall under the heading of non-traditional security, he added.

The researchers plan to expand and regularly update the database and to draw conclusions from the data in a few months. They hope decision-makers can use the findings to defend against non-traditional threats more effectively, or at least to understand them better.

Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin are holding talks in Shenzhen, a day before a first-of-its-kind trilateral summit with US President Donald Trump in the southern Chinese city.

Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin are holding talks in Shenzhen, a day before a one-of-its-kind trilateral summit with US President Donald Trump in the southern Chinese city.

Chinese and Russian news agencies reported that the two leaders began talks around midday on Wednesday.

It was their fifth meeting this year, one of which took place by video link.

Fears over Ukraine and spheres of influence

Thursday’s meeting has raised concern in Kyiv and European capitals that the three leaders could settle Ukraine’s future without them and divide the world into modern spheres of influence.

Washington initially said Ukraine was not expected to be on the agenda, but Trump later said it would be. Xi regards the war as not China’s concern.

Beijing has said only that the leaders will hold “in-depth exchanges on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations” on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting.

According to Washington, the Iran war and nuclear disarmament are also on the table after the US-Russia bilateral nuclear weapons treaty expired in February. China has long argued that the US and Russia should cut their much larger arsenals before it will discuss limits on its own.

Putin and Xi speak at APEC

Opening the event, Xi called for stronger international cooperation on artificial intelligence and free trade. China would pursue “deep-seated reform”, he said, starting with lower tariffs, wider market access and work on regulation and management standards.

Putin, who has been shunned by the West since he invaded Ukraine in 2022, told the APEC gathering he expected the trilateral to be “highly useful”.

With military and political risks rising, he said, “what is desperately needed is unity rather than division... and dialogue rather than ultimatums.”

He also argued that Western sanctions had failed, saying they could not fully halt growth or wreck the economies of rival states.

Trump was still in the Philippines on Wednesday, where he attended a summit of the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). A day earlier he met fellow Quad leaders from Australia, Japan and India for the first time in his second term. The group is broadly seen as a counterweight to Chinese influence in the region.

He said he hoped to hold one-on-one talks with both Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in Shenzhen, adding that Kim “would like” to meet in China.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking in Manila, stopped short of confirming a Kim meeting but said engagement was the only way to resolve problems with North Korea.

Around 2,000 people protested during Trump’s visit, carrying banners reading “Trump out now” and “Reject Pax Silica”, a reference to a US supply chain initiative.

Nvidia reported better-than-expected results, raised its forecast for next fiscal year and said it had no plans to bring back co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO.

Strong demand for AI chips more than doubled Nvidia’s revenue and net income in its fiscal third quarter, as the company sought to reassure investors after the departure of co-founder Jensen Huang.

In its first earnings report since Huang stepped down, Nvidia posted revenue of $115.8bn (€105.4bn) for the quarter ended 25 October, up 103% from a year earlier and ahead of Wall Street expectations. Net income rose to $65.3bn (€59.4bn), or $2.70 (€2.46) per diluted share. Adjusted earnings of $2.68 (€2.44) per share beat the $2.48 (€2.26) consensus estimate compiled by FactSet.

Nvidia shares rose about 5% at one point in after-hours trading on Tuesday.

At the start of Nvidia’s earnings call, board chair Harvey Jones said the board had “unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”. Finance chief Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO while the board looks for a permanent successor.

Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said in a social media post that he would be willing to return if the board thought it was in the best interests of the company, its shareholders, its employees and the US. A “Stand with Jensen” petition launched last week drew support from Silicon Valley figures including SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk. US President Donald Trump also signalled he would welcome Huang’s return.

Huang resigned after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman whose possible ties to Chinese intelligence are being examined by US intelligence agencies, Reuters reported. China has rejected allegations that it ran an espionage operation targeting Huang.

Jones said the board wants to appoint a permanent CEO quickly and will take the time it needs to find the right person.

Nvidia’s future without Huang

Nvidia said data centre revenue more than doubled to $107.6bn (€97.9bn), in a sign that the artificial-intelligence buildout remains strong. The chipmaker forecast fourth-quarter revenue of about $130bn (€118.3bn), above Wall Street expectations.

The quarter includes an extra week, and the forecast assumes no sales of data centre computing chips to China.

Nvidia expects adjusted gross margins, the share of revenue left after deducting the cost of sales, to fall between 71% and 72% in the fourth quarter, from 74.9% in the third quarter.

Kress said Nvidia’s decision to honour existing orders at agreed prices had temporarily squeezed margins. She expects margins to bottom out in the fourth quarter and recover next fiscal year as Nvidia adjusts its prices.

Kress struck a more cautious tone on funding AI infrastructure, saying Nvidia would be “disciplined and selective” about future investments. The company will prioritise easing shortages of land, power and buildings for data centres and encourage customers with investment-grade credit ratings to fund their own projects.

Nvidia also raised its fiscal 2028 forecast. Kress said the company now expects revenue to grow about 75%, up from 70%, from a higher fiscal 2027 base. She said the forecast accounts for how quickly data centres can come online, how strong demand is likely to remain, and whether customers can secure funding.

Kress said major AI labs, such as ChatGPT maker OpenAI and Claude maker Anthropic, are expected to account for about 15% of Nvidia’s data centre revenue this fiscal year.

“Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating,” Kress said at the end of the call.

Meanwhile, Nvidia’s board set up a permanent committee to oversee national security, export control compliance and global trade risks. Speaking in Manila on Tuesday, Trump called it “a good idea”.

Huang faces questioning by Congress

Three US House committees said on Tuesday that Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter had agreed to closed-door interviews that will be transcribed, as lawmakers examine how advanced Nvidia chips may have reached China.

Huang is due to appear on 1 December, followed by Teter on 2 December.

AP reported that Huang is also expected to appear before the Senate Banking Committee, citing two people familiar with the matter.

Antibiotic resistance is rising across Europe, with some countries facing sharper increases and fewer treatment options as experts call for stronger prevention and more responsible antibiotic use.

Resistance to antibiotics remains a major health threat in Europe, with infections caused by drug-resistant superbugs surging in some countries, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) warned on Wednesday, highlighting the growing threat to the effectiveness of available treatments.

Every year, over 35,000 people die from antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in the European Union, Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway — comparable to the combined mortality of influenza, tuberculosis and HIV.

Growing resistance is leaving doctors with fewer treatment options, Christian Giske, head of ECDC’s Antimicrobial Resistance and Healthcare-Associated Infections Section, told reporters on Tuesday, stressing the need for urgent action to safeguard the effectiveness of antibiotics.

“Without effective antibiotics, we could return to the ‘pre-antibiotic era’, and it would be difficult, if not impossible, to safely perform organ transplantation, cancer chemotherapy, ensure intensive care or other medical procedures,” the ECDC report warned.

Antimicrobial resistance occurs when microorganisms, such as bacteria, develop the ability to withstand the drugs designed to kill them or stop their growth.

Despite longstanding efforts to reduce antibiotic use and tackle resistance, new ECDC data show that the situation is worsening as new bacterial strains are emerging that are resistant to several antibiotics at the same time. These are known as multidrug-resistant bacteria.

The European health agency has identified bloodstream infections caused by resistant bacteria as a particular concern, with the region lagging behind its reduction targets, particularly for Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli (E. coli), which are associated with high patient mortality rates.

The estimated EU incidence of antibiotic-resistant E. coli infections grew by 16.4% between 2019 and 2025, despite a target to achieve a 10% reduction from the 2019 baseline.

K. pneumoniae — a bacterium that commonly causes urinary tract, respiratory tract and bloodstream infections — is another major concern for the ECDC.

“We can also see not only that many of the strains are related, suggesting that there is indeed strain transmission, but we can see that they are increasingly getting very difficult to treat because of their mechanisms of resistance,” Giske said.

The target is to reduce K. pneumoniae infections by 5% from the 2019 baseline. However, in 2025, the incidence stood at 3.75 cases per 100,000 people, representing a 72% increase compared with that baseline.

Which countries are struggling the most?

While antibiotic resistance is a challenge across Europe, AMR levels and antibiotic consumption vary widely among countries.

Cyprus has seen a 716% surge in antibiotic-resistant K. pneumoniae infections, reaching 21.29 cases per 100,000 people last year, the report found. It has also seen a 276% increase in antibiotic-resistant E. coli bloodstream infections.

For K. pneumoniae, Romania follows with 18.66 antibiotic-resistant infections per 100,000 population and Greece with 16.28 per 100,000 people.

The ECDC is also concerned about the steep increases recorded in recent years, particularly in Hungary, where resistant K. pneumoniae infections rose by 1,622%. Croatia recorded a 409% increase and Bulgaria a 356% rise.

How can Europe tackle growing antibiotic resistance?

Giske noted that addressing the growing threat of resistance requires action on two fronts: preventing infections and controlling antimicrobial use.

More than 70% of the health burden of antimicrobial resistance in Europe is attributable to healthcare-associated infections involving multidrug-resistant bacteria — for example, when patients are infected while hospitalised. Half of this burden could be prevented through stronger infection prevention and control measures, according to the ECDC.

“There are some measures that can be done at the point of care that pertain to hand hygiene and protective equipment, but also to placement of infected patients in single rooms and, additionally, to effective environmental cleaning,” Giske said.

Action is also needed at the healthcare system level, including ensuring appropriate staffing for infection prevention and control, providing access to suitable laboratory diagnostics and improving surveillance of resistant bacteria, he added.

“Infection prevention and control is about preventing infections and thus stopping the spread of bacteria, while antimicrobial stewardship is about using antibiotics wisely,” Giske added.

But tackling resistance is not just about how many antibiotics are used; it also depends on which ones are prescribed and how they are used.

Antibiotics continue to be prescribed or used inappropriately for viral infections — such as colds, influenza and COVID-19 — for which they offer no therapeutic benefit, the ECDC warned. This unnecessary exposure puts selective pressure on bacteria, allowing resistant strains to survive and spread.

The ECDC also noted that approximately 90% of total human antibiotic consumption takes place in outpatient or community settings.

Infants and preschool-aged children, for example, are frequently given unnecessary antibiotics for viral coughs, colds and sore throats that could resolve on their own, the agency noted.

Preventing infections outside healthcare facilities is also important. Giske cited good hand hygiene and vaccination, which can reduce the need for hospitalisation and antibiotic use overall.

“There are also things that can be done beyond healthcare facilities and system level, and these are some aspects that pertain specifically to the community setting,” Giske said.
